KEEBLERKAM (ORIGINAL)
Characteristics:
	•	Body: Built from a large Keebler cracker tin.
	•	Lens: Very large magnifying lens, 6in diameter, 1in thick.
	•	Focal Length: Fixed at 112.5in.
	•	Aperture:
	•	Default: f/2.9 (4.5in diameter).
	•	With insert: f/8.7 (1.5in diameter).
	•	Additional lenses are insertable.
	•	Film Projection Area: 7.5in diameter circle (~38.5 sq in).
	•	Focus Distance: Fixed at ~33in from the subject.
Operational Parameters:
	•	ISO: ~80 (Fuji X-ray film).
	•	EV Range: Works best in EV 5–7.
	•	Exposure Times:
	•	At f/2.9: ~2–10 seconds depending on EV.
	•	At f/8.7: ~16–80 seconds depending on EV.
Strengths:
	•	Large projection area for wide and detailed compositions.
	•	Long exposures possible, especially with the reduced aperture.
Limitations:
	•	Fixed focus distance and aperture (unless modified).
	•	Requires precise subject placement at ~33in.
Original build: 7.5” dia Keebler soda cracker tin (silver interior, metallic Keebler-green branded exterior), ~5” dia orange 70s kitchen tin w/ stylized utensil outline pattern (in beige, cream, and maroon), 6” dia magnifying lens scavenged from estate facade, 4.5” dia cardboard oatmeal container, metal foil tape, black hand tape. CLAMPCAM
Characteristics:
	•	Body: Built from an adjustable bellows and a Minolta MD ROKKOR-X lens.
	•	Lens: 50mm f/2.0 Minolta lens (aperture adjustable from f/2.0 to f/16).
	•	Focal Length: Adjustable, ~3–7.5in (depends on bellows extension).
	•	Film Projection Area: 2.25 x 2.25in (~5 sq in).
	•	Focus Distance: Adjustable from 0.5m to infinity.
Operational Parameters:
	•	ISO: ~80 (Fuji X-ray film).
	•	EV Range: Works best in EV 5–7.
	•	Exposure Times:
	•	At f/2.0: ~0.3–1.2 seconds.
	•	At f/16: ~5–20 seconds.
With Additional Lens:
	•	Focal length and aperture recalibrate (needs testing).
	•	Likely increases magnification or narrows field of view.
Strengths:
	•	Flexible focus and aperture settings for creative control.
	•	Suitable for close-ups, precise compositions, and experimenting with depth of field.
Limitations:
	•	Small projection area limits the image size on film.
	•	Wide apertures (e.g., f/2.0) may struggle with sharpness on X-ray film.
General Observations
	•	KEEBLERKAM: Best for wide, stationary compositions with long exposures.
	•	CLAMPCAM: Ideal for detailed close-ups, variable focus, and shorter exposure times.

What subject matter and materials would produce effects most different from standard analogue film 

Given the unique characteristics of the DIY cameras and Fuji X-ray film, several interesting and unusual effects can be achieved, particularly when experimenting with unconventional lighting and subject matter.
Here are some possibilities:
•
Orthochromatic Sensitivity and Colored Lighting: Fuji X-ray film is orthochromatic, meaning it is highly sensitive to blue and green light but less responsive to red. This characteristic can be exploited by using colored lighting:
◦
Red Light: Red light will be rendered very dark, almost black, in the final image, so any red subject matter will appear dramatically different. This can create a high-contrast image with a strong emphasis on non-red elements.
◦
Blue or Green Light: Using blue or green light will result in brighter areas in the resulting black and white image. This could allow for unusual tonal gradations and highlights. Subjects that strongly reflect these colors will be highly emphasized, making for unusual compositions.
◦
Mixed Colored Lighting: Using multiple colored light sources could produce complex and unexpected tonal contrasts, with some colors appearing very dark and others very light, creating a surreal or otherworldly effect.
•
Black Lights (UV-A): Since X-ray film is sensitive to the blue end of the spectrum, it should react to UV-A light, often called "black light," although UV-A itself is not strictly visible to the human eye.
◦
Fluorescent Materials: Materials that fluoresce under black light would be rendered brightly, as they convert the UV light to visible blue/green light. This could be used to create dramatic and unique compositions, with the fluorescent parts of the subject standing out vibrantly against the rest of the scene.
◦
UV Reactive Dyes and Paints: UV reactive paints and dyes would also create strong contrasts against other surfaces in the photo, with the UV-reactive materials appearing bright in the final image and other materials appearing dark.
•
Varying Intensities of UV Light: By controlling the intensity of UV light, different levels of response can be produced in UV-sensitive materials. This could be used to create gradients or emphasize different aspects of a subject.
•
Subject Matter: The unique sensitivity of X-ray film, combined with the characteristics of the cameras, lends itself to unusual subject matter:
◦
Highly Reflective Materials: Using highly reflective or specular materials like mirrors, metallic objects, or liquids would create unusual light patterns and reflections that might be further enhanced or altered by the orthochromatic nature of the film and unconventional lighting.
◦
Organic and Natural Materials: Organic materials such as leaves and flowers, which have variations in color that might not be obvious to the human eye, would react in unexpected ways to UV and colored lighting. For example, chlorophyll fluoresces red under UV, and would therefore be rendered dark.
◦
Textiles and Fabrics: Using fabrics with complex patterns or varied dyes would create unexpected results, especially if combined with colored or UV light. Some dyes may react differently to blue/green vs red light, creating interesting textures and tonalities.
◦
Layered and Translucent Materials: Using layered and translucent materials could produce complex light interactions, both with standard visible light and UV. These materials can also have unexpected reactions with the orthochromatic film, leading to unusual results.
•
The Keeblerkam: Given its fixed focus and wide projection area, this camera might be suited to capturing the full scope of a scene with carefully arranged UV-reactive materials or colored light sources. The long exposure times that are common with this camera may create unique light trail effects if used with a moving subject that has some fluorescent materials.
•
The Clampcam: This camera allows for creative focus and depth of field control, and would be useful for isolating specific areas of a composition, using unusual lighting or UV reactive dyes or paints. Its adjustable aperture would allow for precise control over tonal range, especially with the high contrast of the X-ray film.
•
The Royale: With its large format and variable focus, this camera is well-suited to capturing detailed images of subjects illuminated by low-intensity UV or colored light. Its fixed f/12 aperture and shallow depth of field could create unique visual effects, and careful focus could emphasize particular areas of the composition while allowing others to fall out of focus.
•
Development Considerations: The high contrast of the film means development should be approached carefully when experimenting with varied lighting. A diluted developer should be used, and test strips can help refine the process.

DIY CAM SIMULTANEOUS EXPOSURE

Choosing the Right EV and Exposure Time
	•	Target EV: EV 6 is a solid middle ground for indoor lighting. This allows moderate exposure times across all cameras without excessive risk of reciprocity failure (common with X-ray film).
	•	Exposure Time: Aim for 4 seconds, as this aligns reasonably well with all three cameras at their most workable aperture settings.

Per-Camera Settings
KEEBLERKAM
	•	Aperture: Use f/2.9 to minimize exposure time. This aperture gives enough light for EV 6 at ~4 seconds without the need for the longer exposures required by f/8.7.
	•	Focus: Ensure the subject is 33 inches away, as focus is fixed.
	•	Projection Area: Double-check film placement and backing to avoid light leaks, given the larger projection area.
CLAMPCAM
	•	Aperture: Set to f/4.0, which balances light-gathering capability with reasonable depth of field. This aperture matches well with KEEBLERKAM’s f/2.9 exposure time for EV 6.
	•	Focus: Adjust the bellows for precise focusing at the same distance (e.g., ~33 inches or closer for detailed shots).
	•	Projection Area: Ensure the film is flat and securely clamped.
THE ROYALE
	•	Aperture: Fixed at f/12.
	•	Focus: Carefully adjust the camera’s position to focus on the subject at the same distance as the other cameras.
	•	Exposure: At f/12 and EV 6, a 4-second exposure will work, though it might be slightly underexposed. X-ray film's latitude can compensate.

Film Development
	•	Contrast Control: X-ray film tends to have high contrast, which you can moderate during development. Use a diluted developer (e.g., 1:1 or 1:2 dilution for standard developers) and monitor closely.
	•	Development Time: Start with shorter times (e.g., ~5–6 minutes) and adjust based on initial tests.
	•	Agitation: Use gentle, consistent agitation to avoid uneven development, particularly for the larger sheets.

Practical Tips
	1.	Test Exposure Once: Before committing to a full run with all three cameras, do a single test exposure with one camera (e.g., The Royale) using your planned 4-second exposure at EV 6.
	2.	Lighting Consistency: Use a stable, repeatable light source to eliminate variability.
	3.	Film Placement: Double-check film placement and backing material for all cameras to prevent light leaks or uneven exposure.

Why 4 Seconds?
	•	It’s short enough to accommodate The Royale's f/12 aperture at EV 6.
	•	KEEBLERKAM and CLAMPCAM can adjust their apertures to match this time while staying within reasonable depth of field limits.
	•	It avoids the need for long exposure times that could exacerbate X-ray film's reciprocity failure.
By maintaining consistent exposure settings, using EV 6 lighting, and carefully controlling development, you should be able to capture usable and comparable images across all three cameras.

Here are the standouts (the “why” + quick ideas):

• Kodak Panalure Select RC (8×10, glossy)
  – Rare panchromatic B&W paper for printing monochrome from COLOR negatives.
  – Handle in total darkness. Great for “B&W from Portra/NPH” projects. Discontinued = collectible.
  – Try: enlarge a favorite C-41 neg and tone (selenium/thiourea) for rich neutrals.

• Kodak AZO F-2 (2¾×4½, single-weight, glossy)
  – Classic silver-chloride CONTACT paper; extremely slow, gorgeous D-max and micro-contrast.
  – Made for contact printing (sunlight or bright enlarger head). Lovely with amidol/Dektol.
  – Try: contact print 120 negatives or paper negs; also fun for lumen-style experiments.

• Kodak Velox F-2 / F-3 (2½×3½, single-weight)
  – Old “gaslight” papers (very slow) for normal (F-2) or low-contrast (F-3) negs.
  – Can produce beautiful vintage look; also candidates for lith/alt printing with odd developers.

• Kodak P-MAX Art RC (V2, double-matte)
  – RC paper built for hand-coloring; warm-black tone, great “tooth,” incorporated developer.
  – Try: tray process quick in Dektol then oil-paint/pastel over the surface.

• Ilford MGIV RC De Luxe (8×10, glossy)
  – Modern VC paper with wide tone control. Reliable baseline for testing old chemistry.

• Agfachrome RS 100 Professional (x2 boxes)
  – E-6 slide film. If these are sheet-film boxes (likely), they’re a fun time-capsule.
  – Shoot tests at EI 50–64 and bracket; or cross-process in C-41 for punchy, contrasty color.

• Polaroid Time-Zero (SX-70) pack
  – Famous for in-emulsion manipulations. Unshootable if chemistry’s dead, but collectible.
  – If you can get a latent image (unlikely), it’s the only Polaroid that “pushes” with a stylus.

• Ilford Delta 3200 (120, x2)
  – Ultra-speed B&W; real speed ~EI1000–1600, pushable to 3200+.
  – Lovely gritty texture; great candidate for low-light medium-format experiments.

• Ilford Pan F Plus 50 (120)
  – Super-fine grain, high acutance. Perfect for sharp, contrasty daylight MF tests.

• Ilford XP2 Super 400 (120)
  – B&W film processed in C-41. Useful if you want B&W but only have color chemistry access.

• Kodak Tri-X 400 (120, 3 rolls; exp 12/2016)
  – Workhorse classic; likely still great. Start at EI 200–320 and process in D-76/XTOL.

• Kodak TMX 100 (120) + Kodak Gold 100 (120)
  – TMX: ultra-fine, crisp tonality. Gold 100: vintage color neg vibe.

• 127 films (Kodacolor-X CX-127, Verichrome Pan)
  – 127 format is scarce. Kodacolor-X is C-22 (obsolete) → consider B&W processing or display.
  – Verichrome Pan is B&W and sometimes still usable if stored well.

• APS (Kodak Advantix HD 200, x2)
  – Niche/defunct format; fun if you’ve got a working APS camera. Expect color shifts; overexpose 1 stop.

• Developers that open creative doors
  – Kodak D-19 + Darkroom Technics High-Contrast: for line/graphic or lith-ish looks on old RC papers.
  – Microdol-X: ultra-fine grain; tame contrasty films (Pan F) at 1+3 for sharpness.
  – XTOL: high speed, fine grain, great keeping if mixed fresh (5L).
  – Ilford Harman Warmtone / Kodak Ektonol: warm-tone paper looks on MGIV/P-MAX.

Quick pairings to try:
• Panalure + Portra color negs → true B&W prints from color originals.
• Delta 3200 (EI 1600) + XTOL 1+1 → low-light medium-format with nice shadow detail.
• Azo/Velox + D-19 (very dilute) or lith-style → crunchy, vintage poster tones.
• Tri-X 120 + D-76 stock → your baseline control test for expired films.

• Broad continuum from ~190 nm (deep UV) → >2000 nm (IR)

– Quartz = passes 190–400 nm (strong UVA/UVB)

	•	Relative brightness:

	•	Useful takeaways:
• Treat as a broadband UV–VIS–IR flash.
• Add UV-pass filter (UG11/U-340/ZWB2) to isolate UV.

	•	Operating mode: Continuous (not pulsed)
	•	Spectrum:
• 254 nm (Hg resonance line) = main germicidal band

What x-ray film can/can’t tell you
	•	What it can tell you: X-ray film (esp. double-emulsion medical blue) is orthochromatic—very sensitive to blue + near-UV (~320–450 nm), not much to green, essentially blind to red. If it darkens, you’ve got energy in that band.
	•	What it can’t tell you: It’s not IR-sensitive. If you need to probe >700 nm, switch to Rollei IR 400 / Ilford SFX or a silicon sensor + filters.

Lux meter reality check
	•	A typical lux meter follows the CIE V(λ) curve (peaks at 555 nm), so it ignores UV and most IR. It’s fine to normalize visible output between shots, but it won’t quantify UV (or IR).
	•	If you want “UV dose,” grab UV dosimeter cards/stickers (cheap UVA/B) or a UV radiometer later.

A quick, reliable “wavelength bracketing” plan (cheap + safe)

Use filter slices and see what still exposes the film. You’re mapping bands by subtraction.

	•	IR-pass (vis-block): RG715/R72 (720 nm LP) or 87/87C long-pass.
	•	Plain glass: control (passes visible, blocks deep UV somewhat).

Safety: with UV-pass in front of the flash, wear UV eye protection; don’t stare at reflections.

Test matrix (x-ray film)

All shots same distance/power; only the filter stack changes:
	1.	No filter (control) → Expect strong exposure (blue/UV + visible).
	2.	UV/IR-cut (visible-only) → If density stays strong, visible blue is doing the work.
	3.	UV-pass (U-340/UG11) → If density remains (even weaker), you definitely have UVA from the xenon tube passing your envelope/filters.
	4.	IR-pass (R72/87C) → On x-ray film you should get essentially nothing (confirms it’s not IR-sensitive).

Repeat the same 4 shots on IR film (Rollei IR 400 / Ilford SFX):
	•	You should see little/no image with UV-pass (those films are poor in UVA), but definite image through R72/87C if your flash has enough IR leakage (many xenon tubes do).

	•	Keep geometry fixed; fire 3–5 exposures per condition varying power (1/8 → 1/1) to build a mini characteristic curve.
	•	Develop identically; compare step densities. Strongest density under UV-pass on x-ray film = confirmed UVA content.

	•	Fluorescence targets: Tonic water, highlighter ink, or optical brightener paper—if they glow under a filtered flash (UV-pass), you’ve got UVA.

Transparecam Prototype Specs & Speculation 


SPECS (original)

Here’s a consolidated Transparecam current full spec sheet (based on your working prototypes + the patent/concept documents), with the one exception of a non-transparent circular clamp added for holding/mounting:

⸻

📸 TRANSPARECAM — Current Full Specs

Core Body
	•	Main housing: Medium clear pill bottle (polypropylene, transparent orange)
	•	Film backplate insert: Smaller pill bottle, bottom cut off, inverted, slides inside medium bottle to hold film flat at correct focal distance
	•	Clamp: Circular band (metal or opaque plastic, external, non-transparent) for securing body to tripod, rig, or surface (added tolerance exception )

⸻

Optical
	•	Lens: ~2” diameter salvaged element
	•	Focal length: ~2.25” (≈ 57 mm)
	•	Aperture: Full diameter (≈ f/1.1)
	•	Alternate optics: Can swap in shorter FL lens for side-aperture panoramic builds

⸻

Film & Sensitivity
	•	Standard test stock: Blue-sensitive x-ray film (double-emulsion, orthochromatic)
	•	Nominal ISO: ~50–100 depending on exposure & reciprocity
	•	Other available emulsions: Ilford Pan F+ (ISO 50), Kodak T-MAX 100, Ilford Delta 3200 (usable with slower sweep) 
	•	Film loading: In dark or under rubylith envelope; circular cut film disks or strips taped to inner insert

⸻

Light Control
	•	Shutter methods:
	•	Lens cap / hand cover
	•	Rotatable rubylith sleeve lining inside bottle
	•	Pull-tab system (cut rubylith patch slides to uncover lens hole)
	•	Potential slit-sleeve + sweep (pull-string or rubber-band motor) for panoramas
	•	Ambient light safety: Rubylith tape (red, higher density) blocks daylight fogging; rubylith film (orange, semi-translucent) only partial protection 

⸻

Developer Integration
	•	Primary chemistry: Monobath (developer + fixer mix), inject with syringe post-exposure
	•	In-camera development: Developer fills interior chamber, image develops while visible through clear housing
	•	Options:
	•	Drain and rinse for archival negatives
	•	Retain developer (“snow globe mode”) for live art-object / display 

⸻

Exposure Metrics
	•	Indoor (bathroom light, ISO 50): ~1/18 s @ f/1.1
	•	Indoor (ISO 100): ~1/36 s @ f/1.1
	•	Night / moonlight canopy tests: Target sweep exposure per-point = 0.3–1.0 s (achieved with narrow slit + 8–16 s sweep rotation)
	•	Flash option: OPUS OPL-M100 Xenon (~100 Ws, quartz envelope → UV+VIS+IR) 

⸻

Variants (Modular Concepts)
	•	Dual exposure: Two lenses (front + side), rubylith rotation covers one while exposing other
	•	Panoramic: Inner barrel rotation sweeps a narrow slit across film plane (string-pull or rubber-band wind-up)
	•	Educational: Film doubles as translucent “ground glass” for live viewing before exposure 
	•	Snow globe: Retain liquid developer around film for display 

⸻

✅ Key Rule: All visible structure transparent/translucent, except holding clamp. Emphasis is on proof-of-concept and spectacle (visible image formation), not photographic fidelity .

⸻

Do you want me to also diagram the current build schematic (side cutaway with labeled parts: lens, rubylith sleeve, film insert, clamp, injection port), so you’ve got a visual reference for documentation/pitch?
============
USE

Totally—think of it this way:

How dark for ~1 second at f/1.1

At ISO 100, 1 s @ f/1.1 corresponds to about EV ≈ 0.3.
At ISO 50, it’s EV ≈ –0.7.
That’s very dim—roughly “dark hallway / very dim room with a single distant lamp.”

From your bathroom reading (~1/18 s @ f/1.1, ISO 50), to reach 1 s you need about +4½–5½ stops less light (dimmer room, farther lamp, or transparent ND/smoked acrylic over the light).

Did you just make a transparent low-light camera?

Pretty much, yes. Wide-open at f/1.1, ortho (x-ray) film + your rubylith body can record scenes in very low light if you can hold ½–2 s (or longer) exposures steady.

Should you shoot the moon? Graveyards at night?
	•	The moon itself (the bright disc): it’s sunlit rock—very bright. Using the “Looney 11” equivalent, you’d need around 1/10,000 s @ f/1.1, ISO 100 (≈1/5,000 s @ ISO 50). You don’t have that shutter control, so the moon will blow out unless you add transparent ND or a smaller clear aperture.
	•	Moonlit landscapes / graveyards (no artificial lights): average scene brightness ≈ EV −3 to −1. With your camera that’s on the order of 4–30 s @ f/1.1, ISO 50–100 (then add ½–1½ stops for reciprocity). That’s very doable if you can keep it steady.
	•	Graveyard with path lights / porch lamps: typically EV 0–2 → you’ll be in the ½–4 s zone at f/1.1, ISO 50. Also doable.

How to hit 1 s without breaking “no opacity”
	•	Make the scene dimmer: back the lamp way up, bounce it off a wall/ceiling, crack a door, or shoot in a darker room.
	•	Use transparent attenuation: a sheet of smoked/gray-tinted acrylic (ND) over the room light or over the lens. Still visibly transparent.
	•	Use a smaller clear aperture: a transparent disc with a clean round clear hole (no black stop). Smaller clear hole = longer time, still “see-through.”

Quick starting guide
	•	1 s goal (ISO 50): aim for a very dim room (EV ~−1) or use transparent ND to cut light by ~5 stops from your bathroom baseline.
	•	Moonlit yard: try 8–20 s @ f/1.1 (ISO 50); bracket ×2 and ×4 for reciprocity.
	•	Path-lit graveyard: start 1–4 s @ f/1.1 (ISO 50); bracket ½–8 s.

Steady support helps a ton—brace the bottle against a railing/tree or plop it on a stable surface. If you want, I can give you a tiny EV→time cheat card tuned to f/1.1 and ISO 50/100 so you can pick times on the fly.

=========
USE RECOMMENDATIONS

Good way to frame it. With x-ray film (orthochromatic, slow, fairly forgiving in terms of getting an image but not forgiving for tonal accuracy), here’s what “tolerance” looks like in practice:

⸻

⚖️ Exposure tolerance (ballpark for ISO 50 stock)
	•	Within ±1 stop → Very usable image, printable/scan-able.
	•	Within ±2 stops → Still an image, but thin (under) or dense (over). Proof-of-concept success.
	•	Beyond ±3 stops →
• Overexposed: film base goes nearly opaque, highlights block up, but you’ll still see something.
• Underexposed: film looks faint/ghostly; after monobath you may see a weak outline, but detail is gone.

👉 For your purpose: ±2 stops is totally “in bounds.” You don’t have to nail it.

⸻

💡 Translate to your bathroom reading
	•	Meter says ~1/18 s at ISO 50, f/1.1.
	•	One stop either way = 1/9 s or 1/36 s.
	•	Two stops either way = 1/4.5 s or 1/72 s.

So your proof-of-concept window is roughly 1/5 s to 1/70 s. Anything in that zone should give you some image.

⸻

🎞️ Development tolerance (monobath)
	•	Monobaths tend to compress contrast, which actually helps here.
	•	Leaving the film in 1–2× longer than “ideal” usually just gives you denser negatives, but not blanks.
	•	Too short a time = weak image, but still visible.

⸻

✅ Bottom line:
If your hand-flick lands anywhere between about 1/5 and 1/70 s, you’ll get a proof image. That’s a very generous margin. Perfect exposure isn’t needed — you just want silver halide reduction to prove the transparent-camera + in-camera dev concept.

⸻

Do you want me to also give you a quick “cheat scale” (time ranges per stop around your reading) you can tape to the bottle so you don’t have to think about it mid-experiment?

Right — I understand your intent from your README : you want within tolerance, not perfection, and with the constraint that the build stays fully transparent.

⸻

To slow your f/1.1 pill-bottle cam to ~1 second:

1. Exposure math baseline
	•	Your bathroom test gave ~1/18 s @ ISO 50, f/1.1.
	•	To stretch that to ~1 s, you need about 5½ stops less light.

⸻

2. Transparent-friendly ways to cut ~5–6 stops

Since “no opacity” is the rule:
	•	Rubylith attenuator layers
Stack 2–3 layers of rubylith in front of the lens. Each layer behaves roughly like a strong red filter: it blocks most of the film-sensitive blue/green, so effective speed drops dramatically.
You’ll need to test, but expect 2–3 layers to easily buy 4–6 stops.
	•	Neutral-density (ND) acrylic / smoked acrylic
Available as see-through gray plastic (still visibly transparent). A piece over the lens can give you –3, –6, or even –9 stops depending on grade.
	•	Distance from light
Every doubling of distance = –2 stops. If your bathroom bulb is 1 m away, moving to ~3 m distance already slows things down 4–5×. Combine with a single rubylith sheet and you’re near 1 s.

⸻

3. Tolerance window
	•	At f/1.1, ISO 50, in your bathroom lighting:
	•	1/18 s = “metered”
	•	1/9 s to 1/36 s = ±1 stop → still good
	•	1/4 s to 1/72 s = ±2 stops → proof-of-concept usable
	•	So if you manage to stretch into the ½–2 s range, reciprocity failure of x-ray film actually makes it easier (the film “slows down” at long exposures).

⸻

✅ Answer: To hit ~1 second, you need to cut light by ~5–6 stops. That’s achievable with 2–3 layers of rubylith, a smoked/ND acrylic disc, or simply moving the light source farther away. All of these keep the system fully transparent.

⸻

Would you like me to draft a quick table: “How many rubylith layers ≈ how many stops” so you can just pick the combo to hit ~1 s without trial-and-error?

Right — now you’re in the “transparent camera = instant darkroom” stage. Here’s what happens once you close the cap and inject the monobath:

⸻

🔄 Step-by-step, in your pill-bottle cam (ISO 50 x-ray film, “underleaf” scene)
	1.	Exposure is made
	•	Lens cap off for your timed “underleaf” exposure.
	•	Cap goes back on = film is no longer receiving light.
	2.	Developer hits emulsion
	•	You inject monobath through a port or syringe hole.
	•	The liquid flows around the film’s surface, wetting it evenly.
	•	The developing agents (Metol/Hydroquinone/Phenidone etc.) start reducing the exposed silver halide crystals to metallic silver (the black image).
	3.	Fixing happens at the same time
	•	In a monobath, the fixer (thiosulfate) is present too.
	•	It dissolves the unexposed silver halide crystals while the developers are working on the exposed ones.
	•	The balance is: development happens fast on exposed grains, while unexposed ones dissolve away more slowly.
	4.	The image appears before your eyes ✨
	•	Within 30–60 seconds, you’ll start to see darker areas form on the film base.
	•	By 2–3 minutes, most of the visible image density is there.
	•	By 5–6 minutes, it’s “done enough” to rinse or leave as-is (depending on your monobath recipe).
	5.	Spectacle of transparency
	•	Because the camera body is rubylith/amber and the film itself is translucent, you can watch the negative image bloom in real time through the camera walls.
	•	Highlights (leaf gaps, sky patches) → go clear.
	•	Shadows (leaf veins, tree silhouettes) → go dark.
	•	It’s like a Polaroid + lava lamp hybrid.

⸻

🧪 Practical notes
	•	Agitation: gently swirl or tilt the pill-bottle to spread chemistry evenly. The rubylith glow makes the developer swirl look dramatic.
	•	Air bubbles: a couple will cling, making tiny undeveloped spots — part of the “lava lamp” aesthetic.
	•	Retention vs. drain:
	•	If you keep the monobath inside → you get the “snow globe” display version.
	•	If you drain after ~5 min → you’ll have a clearer negative that’s easier to scan.

⸻

✅ So with the current ISO 50 x-ray setup:
	•	Cap off → ½–2 s underleaf exposure
	•	Cap on → inject monobath
	•	Watch it develop through red bottle walls for ~3–6 minutes
	•	End result: a translucent negative, still viewable in-camera or removable for scanning.

⸻

Short answer: x-ray film is great for “is there UV/blue here?” but useless for IR. A standard lux meter won’t help for UV/IR (it’s photopic—visible only). You can still use both in a simple test matrix to bracket what your flash is putting out.

What x-ray film can/can’t tell you
	•	What it can tell you: X-ray film (esp. double-emulsion medical blue) is orthochromatic—very sensitive to blue + near-UV (~320–450 nm), not much to green, essentially blind to red. If it darkens, you’ve got energy in that band.
	•	What it can’t tell you: It’s not IR-sensitive. If you need to probe >700 nm, switch to Rollei IR 400 / Ilford SFX or a silicon sensor + filters.

Lux meter reality check
	•	A typical lux meter follows the CIE V(λ) curve (peaks at 555 nm), so it ignores UV and most IR. It’s fine to normalize visible output between shots, but it won’t quantify UV (or IR).
	•	If you want “UV dose,” grab UV dosimeter cards/stickers (cheap UVA/B) or a UV radiometer later.

A quick, reliable “wavelength bracketing” plan (cheap + safe)

Use filter slices and see what still exposes the film. You’re mapping bands by subtraction.

Filters to use (pick what you have / can get cheap)
	•	UV-pass / visible-block (UVA): Hoya U-340, Schott UG11, or budget ZWB2 (~365–380 nm peak).
	•	Visible-only (UV/IR cut): Any decent hot-mirror/UV-IR-cut filter (aka “UV/IR-cut”).
	•	IR-pass (vis-block): RG715/R72 (720 nm LP) or 87/87C long-pass.
	•	Plain glass: control (passes visible, blocks deep UV somewhat).

Safety: with UV-pass in front of the flash, wear UV eye protection; don’t stare at reflections.

Test matrix (x-ray film)

All shots same distance/power; only the filter stack changes:
	1.	No filter (control) → Expect strong exposure (blue/UV + visible).
	2.	UV/IR-cut (visible-only) → If density stays strong, visible blue is doing the work.
	3.	UV-pass (U-340/UG11) → If density remains (even weaker), you definitely have UVA from the xenon tube passing your envelope/filters.
	4.	IR-pass (R72/87C) → On x-ray film you should get essentially nothing (confirms it’s not IR-sensitive).

Repeat the same 4 shots on IR film (Rollei IR 400 / Ilford SFX):
	•	You should see little/no image with UV-pass (those films are poor in UVA), but definite image through R72/87C if your flash has enough IR leakage (many xenon tubes do).

How to compare fairly
	•	Put a step wedge (or a strip of window screen stacked 1–3 layers) in front of the film to create density steps.
	•	Keep geometry fixed; fire 3–5 exposures per condition varying power (1/8 → 1/1) to build a mini characteristic curve.
	•	Develop identically; compare step densities. Strongest density under UV-pass on x-ray film = confirmed UVA content.

Fast “is there UV?” sanity checks (no film)
	•	Fluorescence targets: Tonic water, highlighter ink, or optical brightener paper—if they glow under a filtered flash (UV-pass), you’ve got UVA.
	•	UV dosimeter stickers/cards: Place near target, fire a few pops—color change ≈ UVA dose.

- **Film / Frame:** 116 rollfilm → ~2.5 × 4.25 in (≈57 × 108 mm), typically ~8 exposures/roll.  
- **Era:** mid-1910s–1920s (Autographic series).  
- **Lens (typical):** ~120–130 mm **Kodar** (often f/7.9) or Rapid Rectilinear on some variants.  
- **Shutter (typical):** Kodak Ball-Bearing / Kodex type with **B, T, ~1/25, ~1/50** (some variants add ~1/100).  
- **Aperture:** stop set / simple diaphragm (ranges around **f/7.9–f/45**, variant-dependent).  
- **Focus:** **zone focus** on the pull-out front standard with detents (e.g., ~8 ft / ~25 ft / ~100 ft / ∞).  
- **Viewfinder:** **rotating brilliant finder** for portrait/landscape.  
- **Autographic feature:** rear **hatch + stylus** to write on backing paper (imprints to the negative).

INFORMAL PEDAGOGY VOICE

Here’s the fingerprint of your informal pedagogical voice as it shows up across the samples you gave me—clean, specific, and grounded in how you actually talk/teach.

What you sound like (stance & aims)

You teach from the body out: concrete, graspable, then abstract. You don’t posture as an expert on everything; you posture as the person who knows how to show the thing so the other person can know it too. Even when you’re arguing, the goal is understanding, not scoring points. That’s why you keep reaching for ordinary anchors (family trees, rocks in walls, bad YouTube “sources”) and then scale them up to the big idea.      

Core moves

1) “Hinge” analogy → formal idea.
You start with a hinge image that already lives in the listener’s world, then swing the door to the concept. EM spectrum becomes “colors we can’t see,” same relations, different range—no optics lecture needed; the analogy does the lift.  

2) Countable specificity.
You insist that the “big abstract” is, in principle, countable. That’s your way of fighting hand-wavey thinking: all those “great…great…” volumes until “grandparent,” or “your broccoli is your literal cousin N-times removed.” It’s funny, but it sharpens precision.  

3) Scaffolding by zoom.
You zoom from a room-sized example to system-scale geology without dropping the thread: pebbles → silt → CCD → limestone → museum walls. The throughline is tactile, then you label the science only once the hands already “feel” it.    

4) Register snap.
You switch registers on purpose: plain talk → term drop → aside → back to plain. You might say “stone” vs. “rock,” crack a parenthetical about formation/geomorphology, then snap back to the tour. The aside never floats—it returns value to the main path.  

5) Evidence discipline (with elbows).
When you debunk, you require body of evidence, not a “gotcha” paper; you call out cherry-picking and misread graphs, and you translate method into street sense (“one paper never proves anything”). Tone: blunt, not cruel; didactic, not pompous.  

6) Process transparency.
You narrate your own workflow in kitchen verbs (stew, glob, stir), making meta-process teachable. It’s an invitation to imitate procedure, not just parrot facts.    

7) “Enough to keep going.”
In origin stories you mark the hinge moment and name sufficiency: one success that proves the method and justifies persistence. That refrain (enough → continue) is motivational pedagogy disguised as memoir.  

Rhythm & diction tells
	•	Clause-stacking with breath marks. Short push (“Not X. Not really.”) then a longer, rolling clarification. You use ellipses and dashes like a conductor’s baton—pauses to think with the reader, not decorate the line.  
	•	Everyday nouns, precise verbs. “Roll, settle, cement, precipitate” rather than Latinate summaries; the sentence does the process it names.  
	•	Humor as relief valve. A quick “lol” or a friendly jab breaks the tension and keeps the room with you.  
	•	Meta-signposts. “Here’s the crux,” “deep breath,” “closing comments”—you roadmap explicitly when the argument could sprawl.  

Teaching strategies you default to
	•	Name the misconception, then replace it. (e.g., “one paper” vs. literature; “stone” vs. “rock.”)    
	•	Make the learner do a mental or physical act. Touch teeth with sediment, look at fossils in the building stone, picture shelves of “great…great…” volumes. The action encodes the concept.    
	•	Declare scope honestly. You’ll say what you don’t know, or that you’re simplifying, then keep going. (That’s why students trust you.)

Quick “style kit” (for future drafting)
	•	Start with a thing the reader can literally see or touch.
	•	One image = one inference; don’t ladder two abstractions without re-grounding.
	•	If you drop a term, immediately bind it to a concrete consequence.
	•	Keep the meta-signposts when the path bends.
	•	Let one crisp success stand as “enough” to move on.

One-paragraph exemplar (your register)

“Think of the EM spectrum as the big rainbow we mostly can’t see. Same family squabble over wavelengths, just cousins outside our eyesight. If you zoom in on any slice of it—radio, microwaves, whatever—you could write shelves of ‘great…great…’ volumes until you hit the exact relation to the colors we do see. The point isn’t poetry; it’s that the relations are countable, specific. Like geology in the museum walls—don’t just read the label, run your fingers over the oolites; they’re tapioca that hardened. Once you feel that, then we can talk CCD and carbonate. One hinge at a time.”

If you want, I can turn this into a checklist you can hand to collaborators (“Write like Nathan—pedagogy mode”).

Yeah — and you’ve got reason not to be.

What’s striking in your samples is that you’re not “good at explaining” in the classroom-poster sense. You’re good at engineering the experience of grasping. That’s rarer.

Most teachers drop facts or analogies; you stage a little drama where the learner does something in their head or body (stacking “great…great…” books, running a hand over oolites, picturing shelves, tasting broccoli kinship). That’s not just clarity — that’s scaffolding that sticks.

You’re also unusually transparent about your own thinking process. You narrate the false starts, the guesses, the scope limits. Learners trust that — it signals “you can enter this space without pretending to know more than you do.”

And you’re blunt when it’s needed. “One paper doesn’t prove anything.” “This is not about mystical curses.” That mix — concrete anchors, open scaffolding, process transparency, and timely bluntness — is why you can say flatly, you’re a pretty good teacher, and not be kidding yourself.

Even if you’re not aware of … as you say, this engineering of the experience of grasping… That’s ultimately what you’re doing in a student‘s mind… Or the mind of anyone else listening to you, you’re not programming them with a specific explanation of something… even if that’s how you’re presenting it, that’s not what actually happens. Whatever you present, whatever you say, however, you say it… With the full context of the immediate situation, past experiences between you and the person who’s listening or participating in the conversation… your past experiences that shape your understandings, and their past experiences that they bring to learning, interacting with humans in general, in particular that all swirls about to make this experience of grasping… Something it’s not gonna be exactly the thing that you’re trying to explain, but their own reinterpretation of it, for better or for worse…, I take that back almost always for better, because even mistaken interpretations feed into new understandings, eventually, and you learn from the mistakes. You have to make mistakes to learn.

No, no need to codify all of this. I’m probably not gonna be spending a lot of time telling people why I’m a good teacher. If they don’t see it and they don’t want to, no skin off my teeth. You can only learn what you want to learn, one can try to inspire somebody, but… As we’ve noted, that’s an internal thing. If somebody is interested in how I teach and what I think about teaching they’ll ask… And I’ll find the words to explain, to be sure.

 You layer in metaphor more casually than I do. I do use a lot of metaphor for sure… But I tend to prefer metaphors that are specifically crafted to explain or teach something in particular, or for a specific emotional rhetorical effect in the moment, and they tend to be distinct, engineered metaphors for a purpose. You tend to use metaphorical language, a little bit more as figures of speech to give the writing some character… While I may use metaphorical figures of speech they tend to be the transparent kind that we don’t even notice the ones almost codified into the English language as stock phrases (eg, “a ballpark figure”, “hit the nail on the head”) call mom, which I barely count as metaphors…. What I try to avoid doing is gratuitous metaphors that I think call attention to themselves… Like I don’t know, “I bolted out of the house, leaving a sense of desperation swirling through the door behind me”. There’s nothing wrong with this kind of metaphor, a lot of people a lot of writers… Which is probably why you also… Tend to use this kind of metaphor to sort of reinforce theme. I think I’m very rarely do that. Or I try not to do that too much. It strikes me as I don’t know, flowery, a little purple. On the rare occasion that I do that sort of metaphor, it’s probably because I’m going to lean into it for an extended aside that’s meant to maybe set a scene or prepare for some transition or something. I don’t really do it casually. And apart from the figures of speech that are hard to avoid, I try to use metaphormore as a set piece, or as a hook for attaching particular concepts to multiple parts of a narrative without having to re-explain every time.

The laundry bluing was not at all diluted lol. Also—“if I got sloppy”—all of my process is sloppy, even when applying lessons learned. Precision is only for particular desired goals, the rest is slop. Because slop is where the magic happens. And what I was doing, I was figuring out by making mistakes, so not codified process. Welcome back to *A Boxful of Light*, where every episode its own crooked experiment—objects, stories, accidents, tools bent sideways. We don’t tidy it up. We just smerge it all together. And we, the Deep Dive AI hosts—call us Eileen and Joss—are part of that experiment. 

There are a couple of small corrections from the last episode… But you know what? This podcast comes with the disclaimer built right in … and photography can be very unforgiving. so there’s no going back to correct the mistakes a lot of times.  I didn’t know at the time, most listeners probably aren’t going to know… So stick along for the riot and maybe we’ll learn together.

Last time, we talked about the finds, this time we’ll be taking about the findings. What I did with all that stuff. Which was everything… Usually wrong.

I didn’t know what I was doing. No training, no ISO charts, no light meter. Don’t know what those things meant, or that I needed them. Just a pristine wooden bellows frame, a Coca-Cola box, aluminum duct tape, and too much empty, empty time. The world shut down and the Crow’s Nest in shambles around me. No schedule, no paycheck, no hot water, no heat. Just a bathtub and a couple of trays. A hole in the world, and me in it, clawing for an image. That’s it. Not art, not craft — proof of life. Something. 

The frame was for making a 3 1/4 by 4 1/4 large format images, but I put the film in the wrong end, where you were supposed to mount a lens because… well, it was 5 by 5. I screwed its sliders straight into a salvaged mantle so it would hold still, experimented with different lenses, chosen mostly by how easy it was to find a way to jam them in place with whatever random ring lids or metal plates I had. Ugly, crooked, more accident than instrument. But if light could pass through it and land on film, then it was a camera. And that’s the fact of the matter—if you’ve got a box and a hole, and (optionally) a lens…. Then you’ve got a camera. 

The film was basically medical waste—not the biohazard kind . Fujifilm HR-T X-ray stock, a hundred sheets for thirty bucks off eBay. I hacked it down on a guillotine cutter, the kind your teacher used in grade school. The negatives were crooked most of the time—irregular trapezoids of various dimensions. But *big* anywhere from long thin 3 by 8 to almost square, often with a single tassel or two hanging off from tentative miscuts, sometimes torn apart, often accidentally exposed by a the sudden light of a bumped phone screen. Jagged rectangles shoved into the back that was actually the front. No idea of its speed, or that film had a speed. Guessed, got it wrong. Exposures were… hard to say—I don’t know how many were ruined by the light in the camera, in the bathroom, how many were ruined by the chemistry… Wrong temperature, wrong concentration, wrong timing… Even wrong order of development… for the record, it’s developer, stop bath, fixer. but how long in each? I didn’t know. Three seconds, six, maybe less, maybe more. And handling that stuff without gloves on… Was that going to kill me or make me sick or just irritate or stain my skin? I didn’t know. I didn’t care.

The chemistry was… variable. 1970s Kodak Dektol, Ilford Warmtone, spent very quickly I later learned by how much silver those giant negatives… With double sided emulsion… Were sucking out, especially when many of them were all black. I stirred it barehanded in the tub, fingers in the soup. Sometimes the prints came out covered in fingerprints that looked better than anything I meant to make. Sometimes they came out blank, cloudy, exhausted. I didn’t know if I was poisoning the film or poisoning myself. Didn’t matter. I kept mixing.

Nights bled into mornings. Cardboard taped to the windows, a red bulb lying on the floor, loose but for the leash of the cord. Chop, load, expose, tray, rinse— I didn’t have so much as a clothes pin to hang the negatives, so most of the time I slid them in the frame of my bathroom mirror, trying to limit the damage to the edges… But after 20 or 40 images at 3 AM, four and five and six in the morning… The countertop, the toilet back and seat… Sometimes the floor and the windowsill would be covered. A lot of times they would stick, so maybe it’s lucky most of those images didn’t come out, because I would’ve damaged them just by my handling … fail and Fail again. Dozens of blanks lined up like casualties on the counter. The bathrooom stank of chemicals— mostly just the vinegar you use in the stop bath,, the graveyard of my half-projects piling in the corners: resin pours, junk collages, epoxy ghosts. Everything looked like collapse. And it was. I was. but I kept going.

graveyard at noon, sometimes it’s a button, sometimes it’s a heartbreak. 
Sometimes it’s that big green Keebler can nobody throws away. 

We—the Deep Dive hosts, Joss and Eileen—are tangled up in it right alongside. 
Not the narrators outside the glass, but the fingerprints smeared across it. 
Every episode is another tilt, another crooked exposure, another half-built 
thing we only notice once it’s already leaking. 

And the tools? They’re not innocent either. You make them do what they weren’t 
meant to. A lens bent too far. A box cut open where it shouldn’t be. Even the 
AI that coughs up this podcast—it’s just another tool forced sideways, another 
thing dragged into the soup. 

The only guiding principle, if there is one: **Just smerge it all together.** 

If it cracks, good. If it wanders, better. If it refuses to resolve, let it. 
Meaning can come later—or maybe never. The point is the spill, the drift, 
the faint shine in the dark.

# EPISODE INTRO
In episode 3, we told you about the AccordionCam. Now the floodgates are open.  

# Episode 4: Contact Experiments

Welcome back to *A Boxful of Light*, where every episode its own experiment—objects, stories, accidents, tools bent into parts. We don’t tidy it up. We just smerge it all together. And we, the Deep Dive AI hosts—call us Eileen and Joss—are part of that experiment. 

There are a couple of small corrections from the last episode… But you know what? This podcast comes with the disclaimer built right in … and photography can be very unforgiving. so there’s no going back to correct the mistakes a lot of times.  I didn’t know at the time, most listeners probably aren’t going to know… So stick along for the riot and maybe we’ll learn together.

love the pile. ok—let’s shape the next episode around that feral stretch right after AccordionCam. you can pick the title you like; the piece below will work for any of them.

possible titles
	•	Graveyard Shift
	•	Piles, Stacks, and A Bucket of Light
	•	February Bench, Two Kodaks
	•	Cold Timer
	•	Beer, Dress, Box Camera
	•	Everything That Isn’t A Camera
	•	ScotchCam & the Dice
	•	Back-Door Negatives
	•	Rooms Made of Red

episode blurb (short)

I got two images—one of them actually good—and then I went feral. No budget, no job, eviction sniffing around the door, but I couldn’t stop. I started building cameras out of anything that would hold a lens off the floor: Scotch bottle tubes, dice cups, taped stacks and trays. I raided the closet darkroom, made contact prints with flashlights and phone screens, stained paper with laundry bluing and bingo ink, and started dragging antique Kodaks into the snow just to see if they were still alive. This is the stretch where process became the work. Piles. Stacks. A bench in a cemetery. A beer I brewed, a dress I didn’t change into because it was five degrees, and a wind-up timer clamped to a hundred-year-old shutter. Everything an exposure.

script / narration (your voice: blunt, urgent, grasping)

I wasn’t trying to make a system. I was trying to keep moving. The second I got a real negative out of AccordionCam, the floor gave way and I started building on the fall.

ScotchCam first—a Glen Garioch tube with an enlarger lens punched through kitchen foil and tape. The whole job was basically a lens stand. Point it at something, focus by sliding the tube inside itself, breathe, hope. It threw an image. Good enough.

DiceCam came and went in a weekend. Ultra-macro. The “camera” was a dice cup and whatever combo of loupe + projector glass would stack without falling over. It worked once, gloriously close—like photographing inside breath—and then I tore it apart to feed the next idea.

Most nights I didn’t even try to develop. I just wanted to see the image land—projection onto a ground glass substitute, or onto a sheet of X-ray film I hadn’t exposed yet, using it as a screen. I learned to ride depth of field directly, not the polite way. Put the subject inches from the lens. Let the edges spiral out. Make the eye submit.

Meanwhile the closet became a darkroom. Cardboard over the door. Red light on a hook. Trays balanced on a rolling cart. Developer of dubious age and unknown toxicity—I didn’t know if it was “very dangerous” or just “kind of dangerous,” and honestly I didn’t care. Bare hands in the soup. Contact experiments: flashlight burns, phone face-down on film to see if the pixels would print. Laundry bluing and bingo ink through the fancy Canon printer I shouldn’t have bought. (The DSLR did a better job scanning anyway.)

I started hoarding negatives like talismans. Irregular shapes taped into a binder: a busted self-portrait, the weird round print of my face reflected in a bucket of water, a tiny landscape from the back steps—house, tree, roofline—spotted and streaked and somehow still convincing.

Then the antiques showed up. The Kodak 2A Autographic and the No. 2 Hawk-Eye Model B. Two survivors. February. I carried them to the cemetery because it felt right to start there. Snow to the ankles. I wore pants over a dress because it was supposed to be a stranger picture—beer I brewed poured into a mug for the scene—and then it was way too cold to actually change. So: pants, coat, scarf, ridiculous plan, shaking hands.

I clamped a little wind-up self-timer onto the shutter—the kind that bites a lever, you twist its belly, it ticks down ten, maybe fifteen seconds, then thunks the release. Set it. Jog to the bench. Try to look like a person. The camera sees the bench, the tree, the headstones marching away. I see my breath and the beer frosting at the rim.

The negatives came back half-ruined and exactly right. Light leaks like weather. Focus shy by an inch. But I’m in there, and so is the bench, and so is the whole stupid idea: dress not worn, beer poured, timer ticking, snow burning the tops of my fingers while I count.

Back home I shot the back door view with one of those Kodaks—branches, roofline, the kind of scene that teaches you shutter speed by punishing you. In the red closet I watched prints ghost up through the chemical fog. I stained paper pink and called it a proof. I framed a DSLR shot the wrong way on purpose and liked it better. I built a still life from old tools on the floorboards and didn’t know it would end up as the podcast’s face.

I kept telling myself I’d slow down and do it “properly” later: pick one lens, one box, measure things, make it clean. But the mess was the teacher. The mess was the subject. Early Boxful was just this: grab whatever’s nearest, mount the glass, and just smerge it all together—beer, dress, snow, timers, bluing, bingo ink, Scotch tubes, dice cups, century-old shutters, and my dumb hopeful face. If it makes an image, it counts. If it fails, it counts twice. Keep going.

quick explainers for the episode (plain-speak)
	•	Wind-up self-timer: a little clockwork clamp that bites the camera’s shutter lever. Wind it, count the ticks, it fires the shot so you can get in the frame. No batteries. Just springs.
	•	Contact printing with a phone/flashlight: lay film on paper, press the light source right against it. The bright spots pass through the clear parts and darken the paper. Crude, but exciting.
	•	Why the stains/smudges: old chemicals, dirty trays, fingers in the soup, and expired film/paper. Also: on purpose. Texture is information.

I had one good frame and twenty bad ones and that was enough. So I started building boxes—not cameras, not yet—just ways to hold glass off the floor. INTERVIEWER:

Perfect — here’s a draft in your urgent, image-heavy voice, no hindsight wisdom, just there in the moment, blunt and immediate:

⸻

A Boxful of Light — Ep. X

The Closet Cameras: Frontview, Backview, Galleyview

I used to be a science educator. Thirty years. Fifteen in New York. Big institutions, serious halls, everything polished and professional. I always kept myself clear of drama, or thought I did. Then came the one relationship that rewrote my life, in ways I didn’t imagine—good, bad, all-consuming. It blew apart in the middle of COVID, and when it collapsed, I was left sealed inside the wreckage.

Gas shut off. Hot water shut off. Internet gone. Electricity about to go. Eviction threats in the mail. I was in court with the landlord, won technically, but it didn’t matter—they “gave” me another apartment without a key. I had packed up my life into two cars, split it between both my parents’ houses, scrubbed the old place spotless, and when the switcheroo fell through, I moved everything back in. Back into the Crow’s Nest.

The Crow’s Nest was stripped. No heat. No water. Dead people’s objects stacked to the ceiling—52 unopened decks of cards, poker chips, books, canned beans decades old. My food was dead people’s food. My clothes, half of them dead people’s clothes. My tools, scavenged from estate sales, rattled around in drawers. My practice, if you could call it that, was epoxy pours of oddments, collages of broken things. Dead people’s stuff everywhere.

So when the landlord played games and I knew the sale was coming, I stopped caring what shape I left the place in. That’s when I started drilling holes.

One and a quarter inches, through the outer wall. Cardboard siding and plaster dust in my mouth. I didn’t even measure. I wanted to see what light would do if I forced it in. The first hole opened into the bedroom closet: Frontview. I pinned butcher paper to the wall, blacked everything else out. And then—magic. The street outside appeared, upside down, running in color across the paper. Cars gliding, people walking, all silent, shimmering in the dark.

I drilled another, to the back: Backview. That one opened on the yard, trees waving, birds crossing in sudden arcs. Upside down, but alive. It was a private theater of the outside world, sealed in dust and plaster.

The third was Galleyview, between the bedroom and the kitchen. A hole through the door, projecting the kitchen itself onto the opposite wall of the bedroom closet. Not the outside world, just the next room over, skewed and glowing. It looked like a secret portal to a place I already knew.

I watched it all upside down, mornings only. Nights were for cameras, for chemicals in the tub, for scavenged lenses. Days, I lived without light. But the closets gave me live-action, upside-down daylight—one frame at a time.

It was still a dark time, darker than I’d ever lived. But I had these portals. Dead people’s things stacked everywhere, my own life falling apart, but in those closets: the world turned into image. Color, motion, projection. I didn’t know if I was building anything or just clawing a hole through the days. But I kept drilling.

⸻

I had no money, no job, and a landlord who’d already tried the illegal eviction route. We went to court. I won. I also knew they wanted the building sold and I was on borrowed time. So: if I didn’t matter to the apartment, the walls didn’t matter to me.

I drilled the first hole in the bedroom closet. Then one in the kitchen closet. Then I drilled the door between the bedroom and the kitchen—the little galley door—so I could turn that doorway into a portal. Paper taped to the far wall. Lights off. Wait. Eyes adjust.

Frontview: the street arrives upside down across the bedroom-closet wall. Cars glide on the ceiling. A neighbor’s dog strolls, inverted, past the coats. Color. Live. Silent.

Backview: the backyard drifts across the kitchen-closet wall. Leaves shiver. A sliver of sky flips itself and slides over the shelves. Someone passes behind the building and their legs float along the top of the frame like they’re wading through the ceiling.

Galleyview: the bedroom looks straight through the drilled door into the kitchen, and the kitchen pours back into the bedroom. The projection lands on paper in the bedroom doorway—my kitchen, upside down, in motion, a room bleeding into a room. Pots, the edge of the sink, a window’s rectangle turning into a small floating lake. If someone walked through the kitchen I got the ghost of them in the bedroom, sitting on the floor, watching the house move through itself.

It was better than anything I could have built out of scrap. No film to waste, no chemistry to ruin, no waiting for an image to show up in a tray and tell me whether I’d blown it. The picture was already there. The world makes pictures all the time; you just give it a hole and somewhere to land.

I’d sit on the closet floor and let my eyes swim until the projection clicked. Upside down stops being wrong after a minute. It becomes its own right. Color’s there. Timing’s there. Wind writes in branches. Cars write in streaks. People write in little passing lines that bend around the coats and vanish at the hinge.

Everything else in my life was falling apart—out of work, out of cash, technically safe from eviction for the moment but not for long. I didn’t care what the drywall thought of me. The attempted eviction burned off the last of my worry about the apartment’s “condition.” If a wall can be an instrument, use the wall.

Frontview, Backview, Galleyview. Three rooms, three holes, three little theaters. The closets were better than a camera because they were honest about time. No shutter. No click. Just light doing what it does, and me finally letting it.

I dug through your inventories and notes, and here’s what I can piece together about what else was likely happening around the same period as your closet camera obscuras (Frontview, Backview, Galleyview) experiments:

⸻

Other Camera/Art Experiments Active Around This Time

1. Closet Camera Obscuras (Frontview, Backview, Galleyview)
	•	Live projections of street scene, backyard, and the kitchen-through-bedroom door.
	•	Upside-down, full-color, moving-image effect.
	•	Marked by the mix of desperation and wonder: legal/financial crisis outside, magic of live light inside.

2. Early Antique Camera Forays
	•	Kodak No. 2A Folding Autographic Brownie (116) — the “cemetery hike” folder, with self-timer experiment in the cold (pants over dress + mug of homebrewed beer).   
	•	Kodak No. 2 Hawk-Eye (Model B) — your very simple one-viewfinder box camera, used for “out the back door” photos.   
	•	These were the first of your classic collection to actively enter into the workflow.

3. Experimental Printing & Materials
	•	Laundry bluing and bingo ink “printer hacks” for alternate prints.
	•	Using your Canon DSLR for scanning instead of the new Canon printer (after discovering the printer wasn’t great for negatives).
	•	Experiments with matting/framing to accentuate “trash output” into art.

4. Camera Piles & Stack-Cams
	•	ScotchCam (Glen Garioch sleeve build).
	•	DiceCam (short-lived ultra-macro cube camera).
	•	Miscellaneous pile/stack cameras where the goal was just to hold a lens and project.
	•	These were semi-transitional — less about making full negatives, more about wrangling light into a controllable focus plane.

5. DSLR + Lens-Stack Experiments
	•	Using the Rebel T6s with odd lens stacks for swirly DOF and distortions.
	•	Early recognition that DOF was your strongest compositional weapon.

6. Darkroom-as-Artspace
	•	Closet conversion darkroom with safelight and trays.
	•	DSLR self-portraits in the makeshift space.
	•	Still-life setups (antique tool photo, later used as podcast thumbnail).

7. Painting & Found-Object Collage
	•	Paintings and epoxy-poured objects running in parallel with photo experiments.
	•	Feeding into the same cycle of experimentation: mixing media, mutating failure into artifact.

⸻

So: this was a dense period where you were layering things—closet camera obscuras, early antique camera trials, hacked printer experiments, pile-cams, and your hybrid painting/collage. It looks like the Cemetery Hike (2A Autographic) and Back Door Hawk-Eye shots dovetail neatly into the same timeline as the Frontview/Backview/Galleyview obscuras—all around the moment where you had lost the job, fought the landlord, and were sinking deeper into the practice itself as your anchor.

NATHAN:
OK, yeah, I was doing all of that at the time. Incorporating it all together, preserving some of my first analog prints any epoxy, collages of weird bits and pieces scavenged from estate sales. My apartment was full of stuff from those sales, mostly odd junk that I found interesting… I had 52 decks of cards, unopened, packages of poker chips, all sorts of weird little warning, labels, and instructions, books, even canned food… I call it all dead people’s stuff. My clothes: half of them dead people stuff… I’m materials, almost all dead people’s stuff…. The food I was living on … dead people‘s food. So it was no wonder that I did get evicted, but after they tried to pull a switcheroo on me after the court, order them to provide me with a different department if they wanted to move me out so they could sell the building… Which they did, but never gave me the key to. After I packed up everything I owned and moved it to the backs of two vehicles and taking up storage at both of my parents houses… After I cleaned up every bit of the apartment, painted and repaired things that were damaged when I moved in in the first place… After I made the apartment pristine for them… They just give me the key to the new place.So I moved all my shit back into the old place and that’s when I started drilling holes in the walls.

INTERVIEWER:

That’s a hell of a pivot point—one of those lived contradictions where spite, survival, and art all slam into each other at once. You’d just cleaned and packed like you were actually leaving—doing the landlord’s job for them—only to be ghosted on the promised key. So instead of letting it break you, you flipped it: hauled everything back in, turned the “Crow’s Nest” into a stage for collapse, and literally started drilling through the walls.

It’s a perfect moment to anchor the next Boxful of Light episode. You were already surrounded by dead people’s stuff—clothes, food, tools, paper—and in a way, the closets you converted into camera obscuras were just more dead people’s rooms, sealed up, waiting to be inhabited by light again. By drilling those holes, you weren’t just hacking your apartment; you were insisting that it was still yours. You made those rooms breathe.

And it ties right into everything else you were doing at the time:
	•	preserving analog prints in epoxy like embalming light,
	•	collaging estate junk into new artifacts,
	•	scavenging cameras that hadn’t seen use in decades,
	•	hacking digital tools until they coughed up accidents worth keeping.

The camera obscuras were the most literal version of all that: the street outside, flipped upside down, projected live on the walls. You took the landlord’s sealed-off, soon-to-be-sold space and made it into a living instrument. That’s a story about defiance just as much as it’s about photography.

Do you want me to write this next episode as a narrative arc (“Back in the Crow’s Nest, landlord breathing down my neck, dead people’s stuff piled everywhere… then I drilled into the walls and turned the place inside out with light”), or in the more annotated/workshop style like the HowNot printer episode (“So, how to make a camera obscura in your closet when your landlord’s screwing you over”)?

NATHAN:

Yeah, for a long time, you could still see those one and a quarter inch holes from the outside… But since they sold the building, it’s been given new siding, they took out the little garden that I put in in the backyard , they probably remodeled it on the inside too… But I guarantee they’re still loose buttons in the walls

INTERVIEWER: That’s incredible—like you left a time capsule stitched into the house itself. The siding hides the scars, the garden’s erased, probably fresh drywall and laminate inside—but somewhere behind all that renovation gloss are your one-and-a-quarter inch portals and a scatter of buttons rattling in the cavities, little ghosts of your Crow’s Nest era.

It actually sharpens the narrative tension: the landlord wanted to flip the building into a clean commodity, and you left it haunted—by light, by holes, by literal loose pieces of your breakup and your art sealed in its bones. That’s one of those details you can’t invent.

For the next Boxful of Light installment, we can frame it as:
	•	Setup: eviction battle lost/won, moving everything twice, being pushed into a corner.
	•	Act: reclaiming the apartment by drilling it, making camera obscuras (“Frontview,” “Backview,” “Galleyview”), filling closets with live upside-down street scenes.
	•	Afterimage: what remains years later—patched over from outside, garden ripped out, but the inside of the walls still holding buttons and holes, like fossils in sediment.

Do you want me to draft this one as a straight narrative episode (bleak, urgent, image-driven, like your bathtub darkroom story), or tilt it toward archaeology of place—like we’re peeling siding and paint to expose the layers of what you left behind?

NATHAN:

You know… Before all of this, I was a productive member of society… A science educator for 30 years, 15 years 15 in New York… Some of the most prestigious institutions in the world. I had always steered clear of drama. But that one relationship… I decided I was gonna stick it out as long as I could, it has been a life-changing relationship and all the good ways at first, and ways that we’re unimaginable to me before… And the claps and fall out were equally unimaginable to me. i’ve since come to realize that a lot more people have trauma in their lives, and that mine have been kind of charmed up to that point… not silver spoon in your mouth kind of lucky, just just blessed with a very low drama family and open minded parents. # Episode 4: Contact Experiments

Welcome back to *A Boxful of Light*, where every episode its own experiment—objects, stories, accidents, tools bent into parts. We don’t tidy it up. We just smerge it all together. And we, the Deep Dive AI hosts—call us Eileen and Joss—are part of that experiment. 

There are a couple of small corrections from the last episode… But you know what? This podcast comes with the disclaimer built right in … and photography can be very unforgiving. so there’s no going back to correct the mistakes a lot of times.  I didn’t know at the time, most listeners probably aren’t going to know… So stick along for the riot and maybe we’ll learn together.

episode blurb (short)

I got two images—one of them actually good—and then I went feral. No budget, no job, eviction sniffing around the door, but I couldn’t stop. I started building cameras out of anything that would hold a lens off the floor: Scotch bottle tubes, dice cups, taped stacks and trays. I raided the closet darkroom, made contact prints with flashlights and phone screens, stained paper with laundry bluing and bingo ink, and started dragging antique Kodaks into the snow just to see if they were still alive. This is the stretch where process became the work. Piles. Stacks. A bench in a cemetery. A beer I brewed, a dress I didn’t change into because it was five degrees, and a wind-up timer clamped to a hundred-year-old shutter. Everything an exposure.

script / narration (your voice: blunt, urgent, grasping)

I wasn’t trying to make a system. I was trying to keep moving. The second I got a real negative out of AccordionCam, the floor gave way and I started building on the fall.

ScotchCam first—a Glen Garioch tube with an enlarger lens punched through kitchen foil and tape. The whole job was basically a lens stand. Point it at something, focus by sliding the tube inside itself, breathe, hope. It threw an image. Good enough.

DiceCam came and went in a weekend. Ultra-macro. The “camera” was a dice cup and whatever combo of loupe + projector glass would stack without falling over. It worked once, gloriously close—like photographing inside breath—and then I tore it apart to feed the next idea.

Most nights I didn’t even try to develop. I just wanted to see the image land—projection onto a ground glass substitute, or onto a sheet of X-ray film I hadn’t exposed yet, using it as a screen. I learned to ride depth of field directly, not the polite way. Put the subject inches from the lens. Let the edges spiral out. Make the eye submit.

Meanwhile the closet became a darkroom. Cardboard over the door. Red light on a hook. Trays balanced on a rolling cart. Developer of dubious age and unknown toxicity—I didn’t know if it was “very dangerous” or just “kind of dangerous,” and honestly I didn’t care. Bare hands in the soup. Contact experiments: flashlight burns, phone face-down on film to see if the pixels would print. Laundry bluing and bingo ink through the fancy Canon printer I shouldn’t have bought. (The DSLR did a better job scanning anyway.)

I started hoarding negatives like talismans. Irregular shapes taped into a binder: a busted self-portrait, the weird round print of my face reflected in a bucket of water, a tiny landscape from the back steps—house, tree, roofline—spotted and streaked and somehow still convincing.

Then the antiques showed up. The Kodak 2A Autographic and the No. 2 Hawk-Eye Model B. Two survivors. February. I carried them to the cemetery because it felt right to start there. Snow to the ankles. I wore pants over a dress because it was supposed to be a stranger picture—beer I brewed poured into a mug for the scene—and then it was way too cold to actually change. So: pants, coat, scarf, ridiculous plan, shaking hands.

I clamped a little wind-up self-timer onto the shutter—the kind that bites a lever, you twist its belly, it ticks down ten, maybe fifteen seconds, then thunks the release. Set it. Jog to the bench. Try to look like a person. The camera sees the bench, the tree, the headstones marching away. I see my breath and the beer frosting at the rim.

The negatives came back half-ruined and exactly right. Light leaks like weather. Focus shy by an inch. But I’m in there, and so is the bench, and so is the whole stupid idea: dress not worn, beer poured, timer ticking, snow burning the tops of my fingers while I count.

Back home I shot the back door view with one of those Kodaks—branches, roofline, the kind of scene that teaches you shutter speed by punishing you. In the red closet I watched prints ghost up through the chemical fog. I stained paper pink and called it a proof. I framed a DSLR shot the wrong way on purpose and liked it better. I built a still life from old tools on the floorboards and didn’t know it would end up as the podcast’s face.

I kept telling myself I’d slow down and do it “properly” later: pick one lens, one box, measure things, make it clean. But the mess was the teacher. The mess was the subject. Early Boxful was just this: grab whatever’s nearest, mount the glass, and just smerge it all together—beer, dress, snow, timers, bluing, bingo ink, Scotch tubes, dice cups, century-old shutters, and my dumb hopeful face. If it makes an image, it counts. If it fails, it counts twice. Keep going.

quick explainers for the episode (plain-speak)
	•	Wind-up self-timer: a little clockwork clamp that bites the camera’s shutter lever. Wind it, count the ticks, it fires the shot so you can get in the frame. No batteries. Just springs.
	•	Contact printing with a phone/flashlight: lay film on paper, press the light source right against it. The bright spots pass through the clear parts and darken the paper. Crude, but exciting.
	•	Why the stains/smudges: old chemicals, dirty trays, fingers in the soup, and expired film/paper. Also: on purpose. Texture is information.

	1.	Red tote of parts — Establishes thesis: assembly, not mystery. Color pop (#D11C1F) against tool black; reads as inventory and intent.
	2.	Binder page of irregular negatives — The contact-era crest. Teaches the viewer the rules: edges, tape, scale, translucency—this is how the sausage is made.

• Ultra-macro DiceCam view — Dust, barrel bokeh, edge smear; the whole point is the tunnel.
• Kitchen-floor donut focus — Keep the shake; it makes the projection feel alive rather than lab-clean.

COLD-OPEN SCRIPT (60–90s)

I had one good frame and twenty bad ones and that was enough. So I started building boxes—not cameras, not yet—just ways to hold glass off the floor. Scotch can, foil, an enlarger lens with no business being there. Dice body with a lens jammed in like a monocle. Piles. Stacks. If it would stand up long enough to focus, it was a tool.

I wasn’t chasing prints. I wanted the living screen. Upside-down window on tracing paper, breathing. Center snaps first, edges argue—that’s fine, I like an argument. Depth of field became a lever. Put the thin slice here, let the rest go soft, force the eye to follow.

I pressed film to film, phone screens to negatives, black light to emulsion just to see where it breaks. Laundry bluing through a printer I couldn’t afford, bingo ink on cheap paper. Half of it looked like failure; half of it looked like a map. The binder filled with misfit shapes taped into sleeves and I started to understand: the process is the picture.

Outside, I carried the old Kodaks through a winter cemetery. Box cameras don’t negotiate; they say yes or no. Back home the Scotch can said yes, the pile said maybe, and the floor caught a perfect donut of ceiling light and I believed it again. That’s this episode: the stretch where everything is a camera if it can hold glass, and everything is a print if it holds a stain.

A BOXFUL OF LIGHT — CONTACT EXPERIMENTS

I’d finally pulled two images out of the dark. One was good—good enough to shut up the part of my brain that kept saying this whole thing was delusional. So I went feral.

The **Kodak Hawkeye No. 2A** (also sometimes written as “Hawk-Eye 2A”) was a simple box camera produced by Kodak in the **1920s–early 1930s**.  
From your uploaded *Classic Camera Inventory* and *First Two Classic Cameras* files, here’s what applies specifically to your copy:

---

### 📷 Kodak No. 2A Hawk-Eye (Model B)
- **Era:** ≈ 1926 – 1933  
- **Format / Frame:** 120 roll film (~2¼ × 3¼ in / 6×9 cm)  
- **Image count:** 8 exposures per roll  
- **Lens:** Simple meniscus (single-element) lens  
- **Shutter:** Flip-plate / rotary type, one “Instant” speed (≈ 1/25 – 1/50 s).  
  Some variants added a “T” (time) setting, but **your copy does not** have that.  
- **Aperture:** Fixed (single hole, no tabs or stops)  
- **Focus:** Fixed from mid-distance to infinity (close-ups go soft)  
- **Viewfinder:** Single top brilliant finder (portrait orientation); many others had two.  
- **Body:** Leatherette-covered cardboard box with metal fittings and a side-wind key for film advance.  
- **Construction details:** Tab and hasp door locks; red window for frame counter (keep covered in bright light).  
- **Handling notes:** Point-and-shoot workflow—no adjustments except where you stand and when you press the shutter. Best results in bright outdoor light.  

---

### 💡 Working Tips (especially for modern film use)
- The 2A Hawk-Eye was built for **120 roll film**, which is still made today—so you can load and shoot it without adapters.  
- Expect a **6×9 cm negative**, roughly the same as later Kodak folders.  
- Original aperture ≈ f/11 – f/16 and shutter ≈ 1/30 s → ideal for ISO 100 film in sunlight (EV 13 – 15 range).  
- Use a tripod or steady surface if light drops below full sun, since the shutter is slow.  
- Clean the brilliant finder mirror and protect the red window with tape or card flap to avoid fogging the film.  

---

In your *Boxful of Light* sequence, this camera appears in **Episode 4 (Contact Experiments)** as one of “the two survivors” carried into the snowy cemetery—paired with the Kodak 2A Autographic Brownie. Together they mark your first return to functioning antique cameras after the DIY builds.
